title: When do you stop polishing a game made with AI and let real players decide?
author: thecrownforge
selftext:
I recently read a discussion about making games much faster with AI and when to release them. It made me think about a different problem. When do I stop trusting just my own opinion of the game?

I'm building a browser strategy and city builder. I use AI for code and art, while I design the systems, characters and world. I can always find one more mechanic to add or one more screen to improve. If I wait until every idea is in I could keep polishing it forever.

Out of respect I think there has to be a first bar before asking strangers to play. If I found this game and had no personal connection to it, would I choose to play another session? Does the main gameplay work fine?   
I need to be able to honestly say yes. A beta can have rough edges, but it should give people a real reason to stay.

Then comes the part I cannot do alone. Real players can leave after a few minutes and play something else. They vote with their feet, and that tells me more than another week of me testing the same things all over. I recently opened a browser beta, with no account needed to start, so people can make that choice for themselves.

I set up detailed logs for player actions, system behaviour, errors, progression and balance. I can see where people stop, which parts they ignore and where the economy or a feature gets stuck. I'm also working on a few simple measures like whether people return or choose to start another task. I can even get to know if they like the game or not. Those numbers are clues, not proof that someone enjoyed the game.

The good part is that I can now make some fixes in hours instead of waiting weeks for an update. But fast fixes do not make a bad first impression disappear. I'm trying to release when I believe the core is good, then let real behaviour show me what needs work first.

How do you decide that your game is ready for a public beta? Did real players ever show you a problem that you completely missed while testing it yourself?

comments.author: DealerIcy3439
comments.body: I plan to make a demo, let’s players taste and dip their toes and feel things out. I also try to make it fit my vision.

replies.author: thecrownforge
replies.body:
I have already 6 players :) And fixed all the initial bugs. What I really like is that 4 of 6 keep playing the game since they first opened that.   
What do you work on?

comments.author: lemming1607
comments.body: you should let other players play your game when you stop developing and all your time is not being able to stop playing it

comments.author: StellarSoupStudio
comments.body: I'm trying to take the Minecraft approach, basically developing in public and treating any and all feedback I get as golden. I finally got a real player today! And they brought up a bunch of points that I'd become blind to. I think the goal is to eventually have regular players or a discord where people can give feedback more regularly while you refine it.
